An outdoor world at street level in a real place: 13/2 Ainslie Pl, Edinburgh EH3 6AS, UK. Open sky overhead. This is a continuous exterior environment that continues in every direction, not an enclosed courtyard and not a picture.

THE PLACE
Telegraphic architectural survey, documentary capture. Sweeping curved Georgian crescent terrace designed by James Gillespie Graham, Category A listed. Facades constructed of pale buff Craigleith sandstone ashlar with fine-tolerance lime joints.

STRUCTURE AND MASSING
Typology & Era: Neoclassical / Greek Revival double-crescent urban palace-fronted terrace, designed by James Gillespie Graham in 1822 as part of the Moray Estate (Moray Feu). Vertical Hierarchy & Massing: 3 principal storeys over a continuous sunken basement lightwell, topped with an attic/mansard storey behind continuous stone parapets and deep classical cornices.

SURFACES AND MATERIALS
Ground Floor: Droved and V-jointed channelled rusticated Craigleith ashlar, featuring pronounced horizontal striations and radial voussoirs over entrance fanlights. Upper Facades: Polished blonde Craigleith sandstone ashlar blocks with fine-dressed lime joints; projecting continuous stringcourses, architraves, and classical moulded eaves cornices.

VEGETATION
Botanical Taxa: Ainslie Place central private garden enclosure containing mature *Platanus × acerifolia* (London plane),

ILLUMINATION
Direct sunlight from a true compass bearing of 253 degrees at 20.2 degrees elevation above the horizon, casting hard shadows away from that bearing at a length consistent with that sun elevation. Light colour temperature approximately 4500K. Clear sky.

OCCUPANCY
No people and no vehicles anywhere. Retain permanent civil fabric: kerbs, railings, street lamps, steps, gates, and mature trees.
